programmes.label: Slavonic Language and Culture (Slavische talen en culturen) at University of Amsterdam

exception.reason: Three independently organised directions were tested. Slavic language, linguistics and language-mediated culture fails because UCR offers no Russian, Polish, Bosnian-Croatian-Serbian or Czech acquisition, Slavic grammar, translation or source-language study. Eastern European literature, cultural history and intellectual life has transferable literature, media, art and historical methods, but no sustained Russian, Polish, Czech or Balkan literature and cultural-history sequence. Russian and Eastern European history, politics, society and conflict has genuine modern-history, comparative-politics, international-relations, conflict, sociology and EU frameworks, but only broad or isolated Eastern-European content and no sustained area-studies spine in Russia, post-Soviet transformation, the Balkans or contemporary regional society. In every direction, extending adjacent material to 23 non-PPD courses would change the object of study to general European studies or global humanities. The missing language and regional content are academic substance rather than professional qualification, so no complete UCR response is claimed.

Its required 30-EC abroad semester follows the current 54-EC first-year and 18-EC second-year gate, including Russian 5 and 6; optional internships stay within the genuine 30-EC free profile. exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Reviewed all 151 rows in the current enriched UCR workbook, including descriptions or outline-derived profiles, prerequisites and Fall-2026-start availability. GOSHIST111 Modern History includes the Russian Revolution and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe within a broad 1815-present survey; GOSHIST312 teaches historical source research through a Walcheren case that incidentally includes Polish troops. GOSHIST211/213 add empire and warfare, while GOSPOLI112/212/311/313, GOSLAWJ212/312 and GOSSOCI111/212/214/311 provide comparative politics, international relations, EU, conflict, law, sociology and qualitative methods. None forms a sustained sequence in Russian or Eastern European history, post-Soviet transformation, Balkan history, regional security, cultural memory or contemporary society. MCCLITR111/112/211/212/311/312, MCCCOMM111/211/213/311/312, MCCMEDI111/112/211/311/312 and MCCHEAM111/112/312/316 provide literary, rhetorical, media, art-historical and research methods without Russian, Polish, Czech or Balkan literature and cultural history as a sustained object. UCR also offers no Slavic-language teaching, Slavic grammar or linguistics, translation or original-language source work. These isolated references and transferable frameworks cannot anchor a coherent 24-course Slavic or Eastern-European programme.

candidateAssessment.concept: Slavic language, linguistics and language-mediated culture
candidateAssessment.assessment: Psycholinguistics, rhetoric, stylistics, media and qualitative research offer genuine analytic methods, but UCR teaches none of the programme's Slavic languages and has no Slavic grammar, comparative Slavic linguistics, translation or original-language source sequence. The presence of Dutch language study cannot substitute for Russian, Polish, Bosnian-Croatian-Serbian or Czech formation.

candidateAssessment.concept: Eastern European literature, cultural history and intellectual life
candidateAssessment.assessment: Literary studies, rhetoric, film, media, art history and historical research provide defensible interpretive methods. UCR nevertheless has no sustained Russian, Polish, Czech or Balkan literature, Eastern-European cultural or intellectual history, regional media, cultural-memory sequence or source-language research. A full curriculum would become general literature and cultural studies.

candidateAssessment.concept: Russian and Eastern European history, politics, society and conflict
candidateAssessment.assessment: Modern History genuinely covers the Russian Revolution and the fall of communism in Eastern Europe, and politics, international relations, conflict, sociology and law courses provide useful frameworks. They do not form an area-studies progression in Russia, Central and Eastern Europe, post-Soviet societies, Balkan history, regional security, Eastern-European current affairs or region-specific source criticism. Extending broad European courses to a complete programme would overstate isolated references as disciplinary coverage.
